_comment: The planet editor's parameter catalogue (plan §5.1, §7.12 setup page): one list for the game's Create World editor (screen/model/EditorFields reads it from the jar as deeptime/editor_fields.json; Gradle copies it like ramps.json) and the browser workbench (deeptime watch, P1-20). Each field names the preset JSON path it edits (dots; a number in a path is an array index, e.g. structure.pluton_length_km.0); a field is editable exactly when the selected preset carries that path, so neither side adds keys a preset does not know. Labels are the lang keys deeptime.editor.field.<id> and deeptime.editor.section.<section> (neoforge/src/main/resources/assets/deeptime/lang/en_us.json), and for a choice deeptime.editor.option.<id>.<value>. kind: number | toggle | choice (a choice lists its options); planned marks a setting whose stage or preset key does not exist yet (canyons arrive with Phase 2; the pack-defined essentials lists with the datapack loader): it shows as not in the preset and the built-ins need not carry it (ModelHelpersTest.realPresetsCarryEveryField); an optional stops list names values worth one click (the workbench shows them as buttons; the game puts them in the hint); integer numbers are written as JSON integers (the seed is a u64), other numbers as doubles; phase3 marks a fantasy toggle shown disabled until Phase 3. The planet, scale and seed paths and ranges are P1-03's params.rs (PlanetParams, ScaleParams, PlanetPreset::validate); the sections `terrain` and `adv_*` (settings audit, decisions log 2026-09-29: tuning knobs that shape the world are settings, not constants) name keys the pipeline presets carry at their calibrated values, so a default run is unchanged; their ranges were run at both ends on a small planet (STATUS.md, build log settings audit); where two fields can contradict each other the core refuses the pair with a message that names the fields (planet.ocean_fraction with the flooded margin: no ocean floor left). The remaining fields are proposals for stages that have not landed (the core validates in the end). hint is a one-line description of a field and sections a one-line description of each section: the workbench shows both under the controls and the game shows the hint as a tooltip. advanced_sections lists the sections both editors keep collapsed until asked for (the game groups them under one Advanced header). Left out because the model does not read them: tectonics.abyssal_elevation_m and trench_elevation_m (validated, never used). Left out on purpose (deposits.max_formed_per_survivor, a cap on the count model; internal numerics and calibration constants, not choices about the world): iteration counts, solver tolerances, tile and grid sizes, time steps, frame and snapshot intervals, layer counts, event-detection thresholds, the energy-balance model's radiation constants, the orographic-rain physics constants and the plate model's Cortial constants other than those listed.

sections.planet: The world itself: its seed, gravity, day, tilt, sunlight and oceans.
sections.scale: How much real planet one block stands for, across and up.
sections.terrain: How the land looks: how steep the slopes are, how deeply rivers carve them and how rugged mountains are.
sections.multipliers: Scale deposits and terrain features up or down, relative to the preset.
sections.biomes: Where the pack's biomes go on the simulated climate: shifts, beaches, patch sizes, swamps.
sections.fantasy: Terrain beyond geology. It arrives in Phase 3, so these stay off for now.
sections.playability: Guarantees that make a world playable, whatever its history.
sections.adv_plates: How many plates and continents the planet starts with, how deep its oceans are and how fast mountains and island arcs are built.
sections.adv_surface: How fast rivers, hillslopes and waves wear the land down, how the crust rebounds, and how the sea rises and falls.
sections.adv_climate: Temperature, rain and ice: how the climate treats the land, and the greenhouse, sunlight and ice ages over deep time.
sections.adv_rocks: The granite bodies that intrude under mountain belts, and how rock layers run from place to place.
sections.adv_deposits: How ore deposits cluster into regions.
sections.adv_biomes: How far from the sea the inland biome bands begin, and where swamps may form.
sections.adv_water: Rivers and lakes: how many streams there are, how wide and deep their channels, how lakes fill and where river biomes go.

fields.hint: Seeds the whole history: the same seed and settings always make the same planet.
Surface gravity. Earth: 9.81 m/s².
Hours in one rotation. Earth: 24 h.
Tilt of the spin axis, which sets the seasons and climate belts. Earth: 23.4°.
Sunlight reaching the planet, relative to Earth's.
Share of the surface under the sea. Earth: about 0.71. The flooded continental margin (default 0.29) needs some ocean floor left, so keep it above 0.31 or lower the margin.
Metres of planet per block, east–west and north–south. Small values make a tiny planet whose rivers and waves wear it flat; the default is 300.
Metres of planet per block, up and down: smaller values make taller terrain.
Steepness of slopes and the strength of fine terrain detail. 1 is as simulated.
How deeply rivers may cut valleys into the finished terrain, as a multiple of the local relief. Subtle 0.5, medium 3 (the default), dramatic 10 (practically no limit).
Rivers carved into the terrain along the simulated drainage, and lakes that fill their basins to the brim and spill. Off leaves no water above sea level.

Block-scale mountain character: ridges and gullies down the slopes along the simulated drainage, cliff bands on hard rock, sharp young peaks and rounded old ones. 0 leaves the simulated terrain smooth; 1 (the default) is the look the planets are tuned for.
How many ore deposits form, relative to the preset.
How much ore each deposit holds, relative to real deposits: its body grows with it (twice the ore, a body 26 % wider each way). The number of deposits stays.
How rich the ore is, relative to real deposits: the share of metal in the ore. Grades cannot pass 100 %, so very high values saturate.
How strongly each ore type clusters into its own regions: off spreads them evenly, strong makes distinct ore provinces.
How big ore bodies are drawn in blocks (length, width and height), without changing how much ore they hold. 1 is the true size at the block scale.
How wide rivers are drawn in blocks, for the same discharge. 1 is the default (a stream at the drawing threshold is a block wide, the largest rivers a few dozen); 2 doubles every channel.
Size of canyons in blocks.
How thick rock layers are drawn in blocks, without changing the history or the ore. 1 is the true thickness at the block scale; 2 makes every layer twice as thick.
Moves every biome warmer (+) or colder (−), in vanilla temperature bands. 0 follows the simulated climate.
Moves every land biome wetter (+) or drier (−), in vanilla humidity bands. 0 follows the simulated climate.
Width of the coast band on land, where beaches and stony shores go.
The window relief and ridges are measured over: the size of the patches of peak, slope, plateau and plains biomes.
Size of the patches of variant biomes (sunflower plains, ice spikes, bamboo jungle and the like).
How readily wet, flat lowlands become swamps and mangroves. 0 makes none.
Magical ore fields and landforms beyond geology.
Floating islands above the terrain.
Landforms no real planet makes.
The materials every region is guaranteed, from the pack's essentials list.
How many plates the crust starts in. More plates make smaller continents, more collisions and more rifts. Earth: about 14.
How many separate continents the scattered start begins with. The supercontinent start ignores it.
How often plates split apart along new rifts. 0 keeps every plate whole; the default is 0.012.
Depth of the mid-ocean ridge crests, the shallowest part of the sea floor. Earth: about −2,500 m.
Share of the continental crust that lies under the sea as shelf and shallow sea. Earth: 0.29.
How fast volcanic island arcs build up above a subducting plate. Faster arcs reach the surface sooner and grow new continental crust.
How fast mountains rise on the edge of a continent where an ocean plate dives beneath it (Andes-style).
How far inland the mountain belt above a subduction zone reaches. The Andes: 400–900 km.
How far the uplift spreads when two continents collide (Himalaya-style). Larger values raise wide plateaus.
How fast rivers cut into rock (the stream-power constant K). Higher values wear mountains down sooner and leave lower land; the default is 2e-9.

How much of the rock that erosion removes is made up again by the crust rising back. At 0.8 (about Earth) removing 1 km of rock lowers the ground by only 200 m; higher values keep mountains high for longer.
How fast soil creeps downhill and rounds hills off. Higher values give smoother, softer landscapes.
How strongly waves smooth shallow sea floors and wear coasts back. High values make coasts retreat and shelves wide.
Depth below which waves no longer move the sea floor.
How fast reefs and shallow warm seas build limestone. It sets how much limestone, dolostone and chalk a planet gets.
How fast salt and gypsum settle in hot, dry, cut-off seas.
Raises or lowers the sea for the whole history: positive floods the continents' edges, negative exposes more shelf.
Height of the slow sea-level cycle (period 250 Myr in the built-in presets) that floods and drains the continents' interiors. 0 keeps that cycle out.
How strongly ice sheets cool the planet by reflecting sunlight. 0 leaves the ice out of the heat balance; 1 is the full effect.
How fast the air cools with height. Earth: 6.5 °C per km. Steeper cooling puts snow lines lower.
How far sea air carries its moisture over land. Longer reach makes wetter continental interiors, shorter reach makes deserts.
How far the tropical rain belt swings north and south with the seasons over big continents. Larger swings mean stronger monsoons.
How much rain mountains wring from the wind, as hours of rain a day. Higher values give wetter windward slopes and drier lees.
Shifts the temperature at which glaciers can survive. Positive values let glaciers form in warmer places, negative values confine them to the cold.
Volcanoes breathe CO₂ out and rock weathering draws it down, so the greenhouse drifts with the plates. Off: CO₂ stays at the starting value.
CO₂ in the air at the start. 0 starts with volcanoes and weathering in balance; Earth before industry: 280 ppm.
How much CO₂ volcanoes and mountain belts release, against Earth's today for the same plate activity. Less makes a colder planet that can freeze over.
How readily warm, wet land weathers and draws CO₂ down. Stronger weathering makes a colder planet.
The star brightens as it ages, so the deep past gets less sunlight (about 4 % less 500 million years ago).
The star's age at the end of the history (the Sun: 4.57 billion years). A younger star is fainter and brightens faster.
How many million years at the end of the history get ice-age cycles from the wobbling orbit. 0: none.
How strongly the orbit wobbles in the ice-age window: tilt and eccentricity swings against Earth's.
How much ice sheets lower the sea by locking up water, exposing the shelves in ice ages. 0 leaves the sea level to its fixed curve.
How stiff the ice is: stiffer ice sheets stand thicker and hold more sea water. About 50 kPa matches Antarctica.
How often granite bodies intrude under volcanic arcs. More plutons mean more granite outcrops and more porphyry host rock.
Typical length of a granite body. Each pluton stands for a whole intrusive suite; larger ones make bigger outcrops.

How far rock layers are evened out sideways, in simulation cells (16 blocks each at the standard scale). Higher values make layers run flatter, with gentler dips; 0 draws each cell's own layers. The default, 10, gives the gentle dips of undisturbed basins; folds and faults come later.

Where one rock turns into another along a layer (sandstone into shale, say), the two interlock in tongues instead of meeting at a wall. This sets how thick the tongues are: below 1 finer, above 1 coarser. 1 is the default.
A rock that makes up less than this share of a layer at a spot is left out of the tongues, so a trace of it does not scatter single-block specks. 0 keeps every trace; the default is 0.15.
How wide an ore province is. Small provinces scatter ore types across the map, large ones give each region a single specialty.

How far underground brines flow from mountains and basins. It decides how far from a mountain belt lead–zinc deposits of the Mississippi Valley type can form; longer reach gives them more land to form on.

Vanilla treats land differently near the coast, further in and deep inside a continent (its mountain biomes keep away from the shore). This is how far from the sea the mid-inland zone begins; a smaller number narrows the coastal plain. The default is 200.
How far from the sea the far-inland zone begins, the deep interior of a continent. A smaller number brings interior biomes closer to the coast. The default is 1,000.
The distance from the sea at which land counts as the very middle of a continent. Few worlds have land this far from any coast; lower it to give smaller continents an interior. The default is 5,000.

How wet the climate must be before lowland can turn to swamp, on vanilla's humidity scale (0 driest, 5 wettest); swamps reach full strength 1.5 bands above it. Lower lets swamps form in drier climates. The default is 2.5, the middle band.
Swamps only form on the flattest share of the land, ranked by how much the ground rises and falls around it. 0.35 (the default) means the flattest 35 %; higher lets swamps climb onto rougher ground.
How high above the sea a swamp can form: lowland fades out as it approaches this height. The default is 150 m; raise it to allow swamps on high plateaus.
How much water a stream must carry before it is drawn. Lower gives many more small streams; the default is 2 m³/s, a brook a block wide.
The smallest catchment a stream may drain, so very wet hills do not sprout a stream in every gully. The default is 50 km².
Channel width per square root of discharge (hydraulic geometry: width grows with the square root of the flow). The default 1 makes a 100 m³/s river 10 blocks wide.
Channel depth per discharge to the power 0.4. The default 0.5 makes a 100 m³/s river about 3 blocks deep; every channel holds at least one block of water.
The widest a river may get. The default is 64 blocks.
The deepest a river channel may get. The default is 12 blocks.
How far below the valley floor a river's water sits. The default is 1 block; 0 puts rivers level with their banks, higher values sink them into little gorges.
How much river courses are smoothed, so they curve instead of zig-zagging along the simulation grid. The default is 8 blocks; 0 follows the grid exactly.
The smallest basin that fills with a lake. The default is 1 km², a pond about 10 × 10 blocks.
The shallowest basin, at its deepest point, that fills with a lake. The default is 1 block.
Whether lakes lose water to evaporation, so a lake in a dry climate passes on less, or nothing, to the river leaving it. On by default.
Channels at least this wide become river biomes. The default is 6 blocks, so brooks keep the biome of the land around them.
How far beyond a channel's edge its banks are shaped into a slope up from the water. The default is 1 block, plus the share of the channel's half-width below.
The share of a channel's half-width added to its bank zone, so big rivers get wider, gentler banks. The default is 0.5.
